title: Iraq Gets a New Prime Minister (But Only Half a Government)
summary: Iraq has a new prime minister, but his government is only half complete! On Thursday, parliament approved Ali al-Zaidi as prime minister and 14 ministers. But they couldn't agree on several important jobs, like the ministers of interior (in charge of police) and defense (in charge of the military). In Iraq, a government only needs half of its ministers approved to take power. Al-Zaidi, who is 40 years old, is the youngest prime minister in Iraq's history. He has never held a political office before—he worked in business and as a professor. Some people think that's a good thing because he doesn't have political enemies. But he faces huge challenges: disarming militias (armed groups) backed by Iran, fighting corruption, and balancing relationships with the US and Iran. The previous candidate for prime minister, Nouri al-Maliki, was close to Iran, but US President Donald Trump threatened to cut all support to Iraq if he became PM. That's why al-Zaidi was chosen. He was born in Baghdad and has degrees in law and finance. Will he be able to fix Iraq's problems? Stay tuned!
why_it_matters: If Iraq's new government cannot disarm powerful armed groups, the country could slide into more violence, which might affect the whole world's energy supply and create more refugee crises.

background_read: Iraq is a country in the Middle East that faced many years of war and conflict after the U.S. invasion in 2003. The prime minister is the head of government, but power is often shared among different religious and political groups.

President Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025) threatened to cut all support to Iraq if a politician too close to Iran became prime minister, showing how much the U.S. and Iran compete for influence there.

Nouri al-Maliki was a former prime minister of Iraq known for building strong ties with Iran. Ali al-Zaidi, the new prime minister, is an outsider—he worked in business and as a university professor before entering politics.
Article_Structure: WHO: Ali al-Zaidi, the new 40-year-old prime minister; the Iraqi parliament; armed militias backed by Iran; and U.S. President Donald Trump.
WHAT: Parliament approved al-Zaidi as prime minister along with 14 ministers, but was unable to agree on several key roles, especially interior and defense.
WHERE: This all happened in Baghdad, Iraq's capital.

WHY: Al-Zaidi was chosen as a compromise after the U.S. rejected a candidate close to Iran. He now faces three huge tasks: disarming militias, fighting corruption, and balancing relations with both the U.S. and Iran.

perspectives.description: Some Iraqis believe al-Zaidi’s lack of political experience means he is not mixed up in old corruption and can finally bring fresh, honest leadership.
Others fear that without strong political backing and experience, al-Zaidi will be too weak to take on the heavily armed militias or resist pressure from foreign powers.
Experts point out that the deep-rooted influence of militias and the tug-of-war between the U.S. and Iran make Iraq’s problems much bigger than any single person can solve quickly.
